blocks.body:
Suppose tomorrow's weather depends on today's but, given today's, not on any earlier day. Or think of a board game in which your next square depends only on your current square and the dice. Processes like these, where the future depends on the past only through the present, are Markov chains. They model queues, population genetics, card shuffling, the ranking of web pages and the simulation algorithms of statistical physics.

A Markov chain is controlled by a single matrix. Probabilities after $n$ steps are entries of its $n$-th power, long-run behaviour is an eigenvector problem, and expected waiting times solve a system of linear equations. This lesson assumes [[random-variables]] and matrix multiplication ([[matrices]]).

blocks.title: Markov chain
blocks.body:
Let $S = \{1, \dots, m\}$ be a finite set of states. A sequence of random variables $X_0, X_1, X_2, \dots$ with values in $S$ is a (time-homogeneous) Markov chain with transition matrix $P = (p_{ij})$ if
$$\Pr(X_{n+1} = j \mid X_n = i, X_{n-1} = i_{n-1}, \dots, X_0 = i_0) = p_{ij}$$
for all $n \ge 0$ and all states $i_0, \dots, i_{n-1}, i, j$ for which the conditioning event has positive probability. The matrix $P$ has non-negative entries and each row sums to $1$; such a matrix is called stochastic.

In words: wherever you are, the next state is drawn using row $i$ of $P$, and how you got to $i$ is irrelevant.

blocks.title: A two-state example
blocks.body:
Call the states $1$ (sunny) and $2$ (rainy), and suppose a sunny day is followed by a sunny day with probability $0.9$, while a rainy day is followed by a sunny one with probability $0.5$:
$$P = \begin{pmatrix} 0.9 & 0.1 \\ 0.5 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix}.$$
Write the distribution of $X_n$ as a row vector $\mu_n = \big(\Pr(X_n = 1), \Pr(X_n = 2)\big)$. Conditioning on today's state (the law of total probability from [[probability-basics]]) gives
$$\Pr(X_{n+1} = j) = \sum_i \Pr(X_n = i)\, p_{ij}, \qquad \text{that is,} \qquad \mu_{n+1} = \mu_n P.$$
Start from a rainy day, $\mu_0 = (0, 1)$. The probability $s_n$ of sun on day $n$ evolves by $s_{n+1} = 0.9 s_n + 0.5(1 - s_n) = 0.5 + 0.4 s_n$:
$$\begin{array}{c|cccccccc} n & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7\\ \hline s_n & 0 & 0.5 & 0.7 & 0.78 & 0.812 & 0.8248 & 0.82992 & 0.831968 \end{array}$$
The values approach $\frac56 \approx 0.8333$. Indeed $s_{n+1} - \frac56 = 0.4\big(s_n - \frac56\big)$, so $s_n = \frac56 - \frac56 (0.4)^n$: the influence of the starting day decays geometrically, and starting from a sunny day gives the same limit. The number $0.4$ is the second eigenvalue of $P$ (the other is $1$), a first hint that linear algebra is in control.

blocks.title: n-step transition probabilities
blocks.body:
For a Markov chain with transition matrix $P$ and every $n \ge 0$: if $X_0$ has distribution $\mu_0$ (a row vector), then $X_n$ has distribution $\mu_0 P^n$. In particular,
$$\Pr(X_n = j \mid X_0 = i) = (P^n)_{ij}.$$

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Induction on $n$; the case $n = 0$ is trivial. Averaging the Markov property over the possible earlier histories shows $\Pr(X_{n+1} = j \mid X_n = i) = p_{ij}$ whenever $\Pr(X_n = i) > 0$. Suppose $X_n$ has distribution $\mu_0 P^n$. By the law of total probability, summing over the states $i$ with $\Pr(X_n = i) > 0$ (the other terms vanish),
$$\Pr(X_{n+1} = j) = \sum_{i} \Pr(X_n = i)\Pr(X_{n+1} = j \mid X_n = i) = \sum_i (\mu_0 P^n)_i\, p_{ij} = (\mu_0 P^{n+1})_j.$$
For the second statement, condition on $X_0 = i$: the conditioned process is again a Markov chain with matrix $P$, now with initial distribution the unit vector $e_i$, and $(e_i P^n)_j = (P^n)_{ij}$.

blocks.title: Stationary distributions
blocks.body:
A row vector $\pi$ with non-negative entries summing to $1$ is a stationary distribution if $\pi P = \pi$. If $X_0$ has distribution $\pi$, then so does every $X_n$: the chain is in equilibrium. Algebraically, $\pi^{T}$ is an eigenvector of $P^{T}$ with eigenvalue $1$ ([[eigen]]). The eigenvalue $1$ is always there, because the rows of $P$ sum to $1$, which says $P\mathbf 1 = \mathbf 1$ for the all-ones column vector $\mathbf 1$, and $P$ and $P^T$ have the same eigenvalues.

For the weather chain, the first coordinate of $\pi P = \pi$ reads $0.9\pi_1 + 0.5\pi_2 = \pi_1$, so $\pi_2 = \frac15 \pi_1$, and with $\pi_1 + \pi_2 = 1$ this gives $\pi = (\frac56, \frac16)$, the limit found above. More generally, for $a, b \in [0, 1]$ with $a + b > 0$, the chain
$$P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 - a & a \\ b & 1 - b \end{pmatrix} \quad \text{has stationary distribution} \quad \pi = \Big(\frac{b}{a+b}, \frac{a}{a+b}\Big).$$

Two things can go wrong. A chain can have several stationary distributions: if $P$ is the identity matrix, every distribution is stationary, because the chain never moves. And the distribution of $X_n$ need not converge: for $P = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ the chain alternates deterministically, $\pi = (\frac12, \frac12)$ is stationary, but started from state $1$ the distribution flips between $(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$ forever. The first problem is excluded by irreducibility (every state can be reached from every other state) and the second by aperiodicity (returns to a state are not confined to multiples of some $d > 1$). For a finite chain, the two together are equivalent to regularity, a standard fact we do not prove: some power $P^k$ has all entries strictly positive.

blocks.title: Convergence to equilibrium
blocks.body:
Let $P$ be the transition matrix of a Markov chain on $m$ states, and suppose that some power $P^k$ has all entries positive. Then there is exactly one stationary distribution $\pi$, all its entries are positive, and for every initial distribution $\mu_0$,
$$\mu_0 P^n \to \pi \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.$$
In particular $(P^n)_{ij} \to \pi_j$ for all $i$ and $j$: the chain forgets where it started.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Measure row vectors by $\|w\| = \sum_j |w_j|$. The key step is a contraction estimate.

Claim: if $Q$ is a stochastic $m \times m$ matrix all of whose entries are at least $\delta > 0$, and $w$ is a row vector with $\sum_i w_i = 0$, then $\|wQ\| \le (1 - m\delta)\|w\|$. (Note $m\delta \le 1$, since a row of $Q$ has $m$ entries summing to $1$.) Indeed, because $\sum_i w_i \delta = 0$, we may subtract $\delta$ from every entry for free:
$$(wQ)_j = \sum_i w_i q_{ij} = \sum_i w_i (q_{ij} - \delta), \qquad \text{so} \qquad |(wQ)_j| \le \sum_i |w_i| (q_{ij} - \delta),$$
using $q_{ij} - \delta \ge 0$. Summing over $j$ and using $\sum_j q_{ij} = 1$ gives $\|wQ\| \le (1 - m\delta)\sum_i |w_i|$.

Now let $Q = P^k$, choose $\delta > 0$ at most the smallest entry of $Q$, and put $c = 1 - m\delta \in [0, 1)$. Three simple facts: the difference of two probability vectors has coordinate sum $0$; multiplying by a stochastic matrix preserves coordinate sums, since $\sum_j \sum_i w_i p_{ij} = \sum_i w_i$; and $\|wP\| \le \|w\|$ for every $w$ (the computation above with $\delta = 0$). Hence for probability vectors $\mu, \nu$ and $n = qk + r$ with $0 \le r < k$, applying the claim $q$ times to $(\mu P^r - \nu P^r) Q^q$,
$$\|\mu P^n - \nu P^n\| \le c^q \|\mu P^r - \nu P^r\| \le 2c^q. \qquad (1)$$

Existence: take $\nu = \mu P$ in (1). Then $\|\mu P^{n+1} - \mu P^n\| \le 2c^{\lfloor n/k \rfloor}$, and these bounds have a finite sum over $n$, so each coordinate of $\mu P^n$ is a Cauchy sequence ([[seq-limits]]) and $\mu P^n$ converges to some vector $\pi$. Its entries are non-negative and sum to $1$, being limits of such entries, and letting $n \to \infty$ in $\mu P^{n+1} = (\mu P^n)P$ gives $\pi P = \pi$.

Uniqueness and convergence: if $\pi'$ is any stationary distribution, then $\pi' = \pi' P^n$ for all $n$, and (1) gives $\|\pi' - \mu_0 P^n\| \le 2c^{\lfloor n/k\rfloor} \to 0$ for every $\mu_0$. So $\mu_0 P^n \to \pi'$ for every $\mu_0$; since also $\mu P^n \to \pi$, we get $\pi' = \pi$. Finally, $\pi = \pi P^k$ and all entries of $P^k$ are at least $\delta$, so $\pi_j \ge \delta \sum_i \pi_i = \delta > 0$.

blocks.title: Hitting times and first-step analysis
blocks.body:
Many questions ask how long a chain takes to reach a set of states $A$, or where it is eventually absorbed. Let $h_i$ be the expected number of steps to reach $A$ starting from state $i$. Then $h_i = 0$ for $i \in A$. For $i \notin A$, the first step goes to $j$ with probability $p_{ij}$, after which the expected remaining time is $h_j$, so
$$h_i = 1 + \sum_j p_{ij} h_j \qquad (i \notin A).$$
This is a system of linear equations ([[linear-systems]]). Conditioning on the first step in the same way gives absorption probabilities: if $u_i$ is the probability of reaching $A$ before $B$, then $u_i = 1$ on $A$, $u_i = 0$ on $B$, and $u_i = \sum_j p_{ij} u_j$ for the other states. In a finite chain, if $A$ can be reached from every state, the equations for $h$ have exactly one solution, and it is the answer; likewise for $u$ if $A \cup B$ can be reached from every state.

Long-run averages are governed by $\pi$. For an irreducible finite chain the stationary distribution $\pi$ is unique, and two further facts hold, neither of which needs aperiodicity; we state them without proof (see Norris's book). The ergodic theorem: whatever the starting state, with probability one the fraction of the first $n$ steps spent in state $i$ tends to $\pi_i$. For the weather chain, the long-run fraction of sunny days is therefore $\frac56$, whatever the weather today. And the expected time to return to $i$, starting from $i$, is $1/\pi_i$. (On an infinite state space both facts need the extra hypothesis of positive recurrence, which finite irreducible chains always satisfy.)

blocks.title: Random walks on graphs
blocks.body:
Let $G$ be a finite connected graph with edge set $E$ ([[graph-basics]]). The simple random walk on $G$ moves from a vertex $u$ to a neighbour chosen uniformly at random, so $p_{uv} = 1/\deg u$ if $v$ is adjacent to $u$ and $p_{uv} = 0$ otherwise. Then
$$\pi_v = \frac{\deg v}{2|E|}$$
is stationary. The degrees sum to $2|E|$, so this is a probability vector, and
$$(\pi P)_v = \sum_{u \sim v} \frac{\deg u}{2|E|} \cdot \frac1{\deg u} = \frac{\deg v}{2|E|}.$$
The walk spends time at each vertex in proportion to its degree.

PageRank, Google's original ranking of web pages, is the stationary distribution of a random walk on the web graph in which, with a small probability, the walker instead jumps to a uniformly random page (and always does so from a page without links). That makes every entry of $P$ positive, so by the convergence theorem the ranking can be computed by repeated multiplication by $P$.

blocks.title: HH versus HT
blocks.body: A fair coin is tossed repeatedly. On average, how many tosses are needed until two heads in a row (HH) appear? How many until a head immediately followed by a tail (HT) appears?
blocks.solution:
For HH, keep track of how much of the pattern has been built: state $0$ (no progress: the start, or just after a tail), state $1$ (the last toss was a head), and the target state $2$ (HH has appeared). From state $0$, a head leads to state $1$ and a tail back to state $0$; from state $1$, a head finishes and a tail resets to state $0$. First-step analysis gives
$$h_0 = 1 + \tfrac12 h_1 + \tfrac12 h_0, \qquad h_1 = 1 + \tfrac12 \cdot 0 + \tfrac12 h_0.$$
The first equation gives $h_0 = 2 + h_1$. Substituting into the second, $h_1 = 2 + \frac12 h_1$, so $h_1 = 4$ and $h_0 = 6$.

For HT the states are similar, but from state $1$ a head keeps you in state $1$ (the newest head can still start HT), while a tail finishes:
$$h_0 = 1 + \tfrac12 h_1 + \tfrac12 h_0, \qquad h_1 = 1 + \tfrac12 h_1 + \tfrac12\cdot 0.$$
So $h_1 = 2$ and $h_0 = 4$.

Both patterns occur at any given pair of positions with probability $\frac14$, yet HH takes longer on average: a failed attempt at HH throws you back to the start, whereas a failed attempt at HT never loses the head you already have.

blocks.title: Gambler's ruin
blocks.body: A gambler with $k$ chips bets one chip at a time on tosses of a fair coin, and stops on reaching $0$ or $N$ chips, where $0 \le k \le N$. Find the probability that she reaches $N$, and the expected number of bets.
blocks.solution:
Her number of chips is a Markov chain on $\{0, \dots, N\}$ that moves up or down by $1$ with probability $\frac12$ each, and stays put at $0$ and $N$. Let $u_k$ be the probability of reaching $N$ before $0$. First-step analysis gives
$$u_0 = 0, \qquad u_N = 1, \qquad u_k = \tfrac12 u_{k-1} + \tfrac12 u_{k+1} \quad (0 < k < N).$$
The middle equation says $u_{k+1} - u_k = u_k - u_{k-1}$: the differences are constant, so $u_k$ is linear in $k$, and the boundary values force $u_k = k/N$.

For the expected number of bets $d_k$, we have $d_0 = d_N = 0$ and $d_k = 1 + \frac12 d_{k-1} + \frac12 d_{k+1}$, that is $(d_{k+1} - d_k) - (d_k - d_{k-1}) = -2$. A constant second difference of $-2$ means that $d_k$ is a quadratic in $k$ with leading coefficient $-1$, and the boundary values give $d_k = k(N - k)$. Check: $\frac12(k-1)(N-k+1) + \frac12(k+1)(N-k-1) = k(N-k) - 1$.

So with $10$ chips, aiming for $20$, she wins with probability $\frac12$, and the game lasts $100$ bets on average. Her expected fortune at the end is $N \cdot \frac kN = k$, what she started with: in this setting, you cannot beat a fair game by choosing when to stop.

blocks.title: A knight's return
blocks.body: A knight starts in a corner of an $8 \times 8$ chessboard and moves at random, each time choosing uniformly among its legal moves. What is the expected number of moves until it first returns to its starting corner?
blocks.solution:
This is the simple random walk on the knight's graph, whose vertices are the $64$ squares, with an edge between two squares a knight's move apart. The graph is connected, so the walk is irreducible, and by the return-time fact above the expected return time to a square $v$ is
$$\frac{1}{\pi_v} = \frac{2|E|}{\deg v}.$$
Count the edges by summing degrees. The numbers of squares of each knight degree are
$$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} \text{degree} & 2 & 3 & 4 & 6 & 8 \\ \hline \text{squares} & 4 & 8 & 20 & 16 & 16 \end{array}$$
(for instance, the $4$ corners have degree $2$ and the central $4 \times 4$ block has degree $8$). The degrees sum to $4 \cdot 2 + 8 \cdot 3 + 20 \cdot 4 + 16 \cdot 6 + 16 \cdot 8 = 336 = 2|E|$, so there are $168$ edges. A corner has degree $2$, so the expected return time is $336/2 = 168$ moves.

The knight's walk is periodic (every move changes the colour of the square), so $(P^n)_{ii}$ does not converge; the return-time formula does not need aperiodicity.

blocks.body:
- Conventions: here $p_{ij}$ is the probability of moving from $i$ to $j$, rows sum to $1$, and distributions are row vectors multiplied on the left, $\mu P$. Some books use the transpose; mixing the two conventions transposes everything.
- The Markov property is not independence. Consecutive states are usually strongly dependent; what is required is that, given the present, the past gives no further information.
- A function of a Markov chain is usually not a Markov chain. If a chain cycles $1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 1$ and you record only whether it is in $\{1, 2\}$, then after two steps in $\{1, 2\}$ the next step surely leaves it, while after $3$ and one step in $\{1, 2\}$ it surely stays: the past matters.
- Expected hitting times can be far from typical ones. In gambler's ruin with $k = 1$ and $N = 100$ the expected number of bets is $99$, but with probability $\frac12$ the game ends after the first bet.

Computing $P^n$ is a job for [[diagonalization]]: if $P = VDV^{-1}$ then $P^n = VD^nV^{-1}$, and the second-largest eigenvalue in absolute value (the $0.4$ of the weather chain) sets the speed of convergence. For reversible chains, those with $\pi_i p_{ij} = \pi_j p_{ji}$ such as random walks on graphs, $P$ is self-adjoint for the inner product weighted by $\pi$, so the [[spectral-theorem]] gives real eigenvalues and an orthogonal eigenbasis. This is the starting point of the theory of mixing times, which answers questions such as how many riffle shuffles randomise a deck of $52$ cards (about seven, by a theorem of Bayer and Diaconis for the standard Gilbert–Shannon–Reeds model of a riffle shuffle).

The ergodic theorem is the Markov-chain version of the law of large numbers in [[limit-theorems]], and in continuous-time chains the waiting times between jumps are exponential ([[distributions]]). Markov chain Monte Carlo, such as the Metropolis algorithm, samples from a complicated distribution $\pi$ by running a chain designed to have $\pi$ as its stationary distribution; it is a basic tool of statistical physics, Bayesian statistics and approximate counting in computer science.

1. For $P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 - a & a \\ b & 1 - b \end{pmatrix}$ with $0 < a + b < 2$, show that $(P^n)_{11} = \frac{b}{a+b} + \frac{a}{a+b}(1 - a - b)^n$.
2. A fair die is rolled until two sixes appear in a row. Find the expected number of rolls.
3. A particle performs a random walk on the vertices of a cube, moving along a uniformly random edge at each step. Find the expected number of steps to reach the opposite vertex.
4. Show that if every column of a stochastic matrix $P$ also sums to $1$, then the uniform distribution is stationary.
